title: There's No "Arriving"
html:
Remember all the times you thought your life would dramatically improve once you reached some goal?

Remember all the times that didn’t happen?

Me too.

Endpoints almost always prove to be mirages.

The graduation,

the pay raise,

the completion of a project,

the retirement…

Such highs leave little more than faint imprints in our minds that wash away like footprints in the sand.

After we take off your cap and gown, rack the weight after a new squat PR, or get that promotion at work, we feel great… for a time. Then, we recognize that we still have the same insecurities, the same crippling thought patterns, and the same habits that lie at the root of our suffering.

According to Harvard researchers involved in the Harvard Study of Adult Development, the longest-running study of adult well-being, circumstance accounts for only a small amount of the variance in our happiness1 levels, with much of the variance being accounted for by how we engage with the world. Pulling directly from The Harvard Gazette, such things include:

  • Being physically active

  • Maintaining healthy habits

  • Exercising mature coping mechanisms

  • Having stable relationships

Contrast this with things we often think will make us happier:

  • Getting a pay raise

  • Getting new clothes/shoes

  • Getting nicer cars

  • Getting higher status jobs

Notice how the items on the list of things that actually make us happier are continuous processes, whereas the items on the list of things we think will make us happier are discrete events. If continuous processes are synonymous with journeys, and discrete events are synonymous with destinations, then what the Harvard Study of Adult Development illustrates through over 80 years of data is that, indeed, life is about the journey, not the destination. Cliche, yes. But cliches are cliches for a reason.

As much as we want to roll our eyes and scoff at the people (like me! hahaha) who tell us to slow down and learn to enjoy the journey, there’s deep wisdom in such recommendations.

There is no arriving. No final destination (except death, perhaps).

The journey is all we’ve got.

Why not make it a happy one?

As for the intermediate destinations along the way, refer to Mr. Incredible above.

1

Talk of happiness always seems to come with confusion about what “happiness” means. In the Harvard Study of Adult Development, “happiness” seems synonymous with contentment, whereas others may think it synonymous with “joyfulness.” States of contentment are sustainable, while joyous highs are not. So, for this post, I’ll refer to happiness as a synonym for contentment.
